1) ultrafast MAS (60 kHz) enables the detection of fully protonated microcrystallized proteins in the solid-state; 2) this approach enables to obtain narrow 1H Nmr lineshapes for 1H,15N,13Cα and 13C=O resonances; 3) the 1H chemical shift information is sufficient for the backbone assignment; 4) 1H-13C and 1H-15N dip
ultrafast magic-angle-spun 1H-detected NMR spectra of solid proteins are characterized by narrow linewidths and can be used to obtain backbone 1H assignments.

the combination of ultrafast MAS and 1H-detection NMR spectroscopy allows for the first time to record high-resolution 1H NAR spectra of microcrystallized and noncrystallyzed fully protonated proteins in the solid state.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel NMR techniques for the investigation of biological macromolecules and the application of these techniques in structural biology and biophysics.
the application of solid state NMR to the structural analysis of membrane proteins and protein complexes.
the application of solid state NMR to the study of the molecular dynamics in proteins and peptides in order to understand the molecular basis of their biological function.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the use of 1H detection for the analysis of fully protonated proteins in the solid state is a promising tool for structural investigations of microcrystallines and noncrystalli- ne proteins, which is particularly useful for the characterization of proteins that cannot be studied by solution NMR.
the use of ultrafast MAS NMR is a very useful and promising tool for the study of solid proteins.
the use of 13C-1H HSQC experiments in combination with 1D 1H spectra provides a powerful tool for the analysis of fully protonated microcrystallized or noncrystallized proteins in the solid state.

we have demonstrated that 1H detection is feasible for solid proteins.
we have shown how to obtain narrow proton linewidths for fully protonated proteins in the solid state.
it is possible to get high resolution 1H spectra for fully protonated proteins in the solid state, and this can be done with a standard 600 MHz spectrometer.
